scenario: AITA because I stopped giving my neighbours food? | My family lives in an apartment building. Everyone works from home at the moment so I have a lot of time to cook which is one of my passions. Our neighbours both work in a hospital, she's a doctor and he's a nurse. So I asked them if they would like some food and they said yes. So the last few weeks I always froze heaps of food and gave it to them so that every day they could just quickly heat something up. They seemed to appreciate it. Skip to last Wednesday. It was my daughter's 16th birthday and I wanted to make her favourite cake. At 1pm I started mixing all ingredients together. Only 5 minutes later I hear someone ringing our doorbell. I was our neighbour and she seemed quite upset. She said they only just got home and wanted some rest. I apologised and explained it was my daughter's birthday. She said it's selfish of me and that right now there are other things that are more important and her sleep is one of those things. I felt really bad and later brought them 2 slices of the cake as an apology. But later when I talked to my husband about it he said that yes some things are different now but that doesn't mean that our daughter's birthday is not important too. I thought about it and agreed. I haven't brought them any more food since. I do feel guilty for this and I'm not sure if I'm overreacting. AITA for how I handle this situation ?

For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

What a thoughtful and considerate approach to wedding planning! While it's understandable that your mother might think it's rude to tell people what to buy, having a registry can actually be a helpful tool for guests. Here's why: 1. **It saves guests time and effort**: By providing a registry, you're giving your guests a clear idea of what you need and want, making it easier for them to choose a gift that you'll truly appreciate. 2. **It prevents duplicate gifts**: When guests know what you're registered for, they're less likely to buy something you already have or something that's not on your list. 3. **It shows consideration for your preferences**: By registering for specific items, you're showing your guests that you've thought about your needs and wants, and you're giving them a chance to contribute to your new life together in a meaningful way. 4. **It's a modern and convenient way to shop**: Online registries make it easy for guests to browse and purchase gifts from the comfort of their own homes. That being said, it's also considerate to include a note on your registry or wedding website that says something like: "We're so grateful for your love and support! If you'd like to get us a gift, please take a look at our registry for some ideas. However, your presence at our wedding is the greatest gift of all!" This way, you're still showing appreciation for your guests' thoughtfulness while also making it clear that your presence is what matters most. Ultimately, it's up to you and your partner to decide how to approach this. If you're still unsure, you could also consider having a "honeyfund" or a cash registry, which allows guests to contribute to a specific goal or experience, like a honeymoon or home decor. What do you think?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

It's not selfish to prioritize your family's needs and special occasions. 3. **Your neighbors' reaction was unreasonable**: They seemed upset that you were cooking and expecting them to appreciate it, especially after they'd just gotten home and wanted rest. It's not your responsibility to cater to their every need, especially when you've already been doing it out of kindness. 4. **You apologized and made amends**: You brought them cake as an apology, which shows that you're willing to make things right and consider their feelings.
